## 之后的热图统一用**按样本的 z-score**：把每个样本在 300 个基因上标准化
## （`scale()` 默认按列，即按样本），再取回长表。`z_sample` 是这一列的列名。
data(airway_heatmap, package = "ggutils")
airway_sample_z <- local({
  m <- tapply(airway_heatmap$df$z,
              list(airway_heatmap$df$gene, airway_heatmap$df$sample), mean)
  m <- scale(m)                                   # column-wise = per sample
  out <- as.data.frame(as.table(m))
  names(out) <- c("gene", "sample", "z_sample")
  out <- merge(out, airway_heatmap$genes[c("gene", "gene_set")], by = "gene")
  out$gene <- factor(out$gene, levels = rev(airway_heatmap$genes$gene))
  out$sample <- factor(out$sample, levels = airway_heatmap$samples$sample)
  out$gene_set <- factor(out$gene_set, levels = levels(airway_heatmap$df$gene_set))
  out
})
```

# What ggutils is

`ggutils` is a `ggplot2` extension for **everything that sits next to the axis**.

`ggplot2` draws panels, ticks and legends beautifully, but a few everyday situations
still force you into hand-written `theme()` calls, `gtable` surgery, or simply giving
up: 50 or 200 levels on a discrete axis piling up into an unreadable block; a cluster
tree that has to hang beside a discrete axis with its leaves in the same order as the
labels; facets where every panel should be scaled to its own data.

`ggutils` collects those into a handful of `guide_*()`, `scale_*()` and `facet_*()`
functions, and it stays inside the `ggplot2` idiom — your layers and `theme()` are
untouched, only the axis and facet layer gains something.

| What you are facing | What to reach for |
|---|---|
| Crowded categorical labels, you only want a few | `guide_axis_smart()` with `n =` / `which =` / `nrow =` |
| The labels you kept must point back to their ticks | the leader lines of `guide_axis_smart()` (`connection_style`) |
| A cluster tree beside a discrete axis, leaves in label order | `guide_axis_cluster()` / `scale_x_cluster()` / `scale_y_cluster()` |
| Per-panel scales, axes and trees after faceting | `facet_gridn()` |
| Hundreds of labels that will not fit on a line | `coord_spiral()` / `scale_x_spiral_axis()` |
| The tree gets squeezed out of the facet strip | `strip_cluster()` |
| You only want the layout algorithms | `box_arrange()` / `smart_align()` / `smart_stack()` |

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("junjunlab/ggutils")
```

Once installed, one extra `guides()` line on any plot is enough — see the comparison
in the next section.

A suggested reading order: two short sections to see "crowded" versus "not crowded",
then a section per argument of `guide_axis_smart()`; the y axis, radial coordinates,
heatmap annotation and long labels each get their own section; facets and
`facet_gridn()` come next; cluster trees and the known limitations close the
document.

# The problem: crowded labels

`ggplot2` draws a tick and a label for **every** level of a discrete axis. With many categories (50 samples, 200 features) the labels pile up under the axis: at best they overlap and become unreadable, at worst you delete them and lose the information. Rotating them by 90 degrees helps a little, but long labels and many categories still run off the panel.

```{r data}
set.seed(2024)
df50 <- data.frame(
  sample = factor(paste0("Sample", 1:50), levels = paste0("Sample", 1:50)),
  value = round(runif(50, 10, 100), 1)
)
```

```{r motivation, fig.cap = "The default x axis with 50 discrete levels: the labels overlap and cannot be read"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Default axis: 50 labels in a pile") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

`ggutils` provides `guide_axis_smart()`. It takes over label drawing on a discrete axis and does three things:

1. **Show only the labels you care about** (`which =` / `n =`). Every other tick is still connected to its meaning by a **leader line**, so the correspondence stays obvious.
2. **Spread the labels over several rows (x axis) or columns (y axis)** outside the axis, using the page space that a default axis wastes.
3. **Never overlap labels**: when there is not enough room it displays fewer labels instead of drawing a pile.

# Quick start

Add one `guides()` line to an existing plot:

```{r quickstart, fig.cap = "guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2): only 10 labels, two staggered rows, each tied back to its tick"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

Only three things change: load the package, add `guides(x = guide_axis_smart(...))`, keep the rest. Note that you do **not** need `theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())` — the guide draws the labels itself.

## Two ways to attach the guide

`guide_axis_smart()` can go into `guides()` or into the `guide` argument of a scale (under `coord_flip()` the two are not equivalent, see below):

```{r two-ways, fig.cap = "Both spellings give the same plot: guides(x = ...) on top, scale_x_discrete(guide = ...) below"}
p_guides <- ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 8, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Style 1: guides(x = guide_axis_smart(...))") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)

p_scale <- ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis_smart(n = 8, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Style 2: scale_x_discrete(guide = ...)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)

p_guides
p_scale
```

# Parameter reference: what every argument does

The arguments fall into four groups: **which labels**, **how they are laid
out**, **how the leader lines are drawn**, and **the rest, passed on to
`guide_axis()`**. In practice you only touch five of them: `which`, `n`,
`nrow`, `connection_style` and `angle`.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Which labels** | | |
| `which` | `NULL` | labels to show: integer indices / label text / logical vector / function. `NULL` shows as many as fit |
| `n` | `NULL` | maximum number of labels. With `which = NULL`, `n` evenly spaced labels are picked; with `which`, the selection is truncated to `n` |
| **Layout** | | |
| `nrow` | `NULL` | number of parallel tracks: rows on an x axis, columns on a y axis. `NULL` is automatic: one track while everything fits, more only when labels crowd together |
| `padding` | `0.25` | minimum gap between two label boxes in a track, as a fraction of the label height; on a radial axis it is the gap along the arc |
| `gap` | `0.30` | gap between two neighbouring tracks (relative to label height) |
| `extend` | `0` | how far a label may be pushed beyond the axis range (0 to 0.5). `0` keeps every label inside the panel; larger values need enough `plot.margin` |
| `panel_width` | `NULL` | panel width (x axis) or height (y axis) in cm, assumed when estimating the number of tracks; `NULL` estimates it from the device |
| `max_nrow` | `8L` | upper bound for the automatic number of tracks |
| **Leader lines** | | |
| `connection` | `TRUE` | draw leader lines? |
| `connection_style` | `"diagonal"` | `"diagonal"` (short stub, diagonal, short stub -- the circlize / `anno_mark()` shape), `"straight"` (one line), `"elbow"` (perpendicular plus a shelf) |
| `link_length` | `3` | length in mm of the leader between the axis and the first track; on a radial axis, the distance between the circle and the label |
| `connection_col` | `NULL` | leader colour; `NULL` takes the tick colour |
| `connection_lwd` | `0.5` | leader width |
| `connection_lty` | `1` | leader line type |
| **Ticks and text** | | |
| `tick` | `"all"` | `"all"` ticks, `"shown"` only the ticks of drawn labels, `"none"` no ticks |
| `angle` | `NULL` | label rotation in degrees; `NULL` inherits the theme |
| `hjust`, `vjust` | `NULL` | label justification inside its box; `NULL` centres it, which keeps the leader on the visual centre of the text |
| **Radial only** | | |
| `theta_side` | `"outside"` | labels outside the circle (`"outside"`) or attached to the inner ring of `coord_radial(inner.radius =)` (`"inside"`) |
| **Passed to `guide_axis()`** | | |
| `title` | `waiver()` | axis title |
| `minor.ticks` | `FALSE` | draw minor ticks |
| `cap` | `"none"` | axis line end style |
| `order` | `0` | drawing order among guides |
| `position` | `waiver()` | axis position (top/bottom/left/right); rarely changed |
| `theme` | `NULL` | theme elements that apply to this guide only |

Four combinations that cover most plots:

```r
# 8 genes out of 200, one track
guides(y = guide_axis_smart(which = c("TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS",
                                      "BRCA1", "PTEN", "RB1", "ALK")))

# 50 samples, at most 10 labels, staggered over two rows
guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2))

# long labels, crowded: extra tracks plus longer leader lines
guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = 1:40, nrow = 3,
                            connection_style = "diagonal", link_length = 5))

# circular heatmap: labels outside the ring, 20 genes only
guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = mark, theta_side = "outside"))
```

# Show only the labels you want: four forms of `which`

`which` decides which labels are displayed. It accepts four forms:

| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Integer vector | indices into the breaks of the scale | `which = seq(1, 50, by = 10)` |
| Character vector | exact match on the label text | `which = c("Sample1", "Sample25", "Sample50")` |
| Logical vector | one entry per label, `TRUE` keeps it | `which = grepl("0$", levels(sample))` |
| Function | `function(labels, positions)` returning a logical vector | `which = function(labels, positions) positions > 0.45 & positions < 0.55` |

`positions` is the **relative position** of a label inside the panel (0 to 1 along the axis). It does not depend on the data values and is handy for position-based rules.

## Integer indices

```{r which-integer, fig.cap = "which = seq(1, 50, by = 10): every tenth label"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = seq(1, 50, by = 10), nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "which = seq(1, 50, by = 10)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

## Character vector

```{r which-character, fig.cap = "Matching label text: the four labels Sample1, Sample2, Sample25 and Sample50"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(
    which = c("Sample1", "Sample2", "Sample25", "Sample50"),
    nrow = 1
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Match label text: which = c(\"Sample1\", \"Sample2\", \"Sample25\", \"Sample50\")") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

## Logical vector

```{r which-logical, fig.cap = "A logical vector: only samples whose number ends in 0"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(
    which = grepl("0$", levels(df50$sample)),
    nrow = 1
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Logical vector: which = grepl(\"0$\", levels(sample))") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

## Function

When `which` is a function, it is called with the label texts and the relative positions and must return a logical vector (index vectors are also accepted). The example keeps every tenth label:

```{r which-function, fig.cap = "which = function(labels, positions) seq_along(labels) %% 10 == 1: every tenth label"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(
    which = function(labels, positions) seq_along(labels) %% 10 == 1,
    nrow = 2
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Function: every tenth label") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

The function form is most useful for **position-based** selection: `positions` runs from 0 to 1, so `positions > 0.9` keeps only the right-hand end of the axis.

# Automatic selection: `n`

If you do not want to compute indices, just cap the number of labels:

```{r n-5, fig.cap = "n = 5: five evenly spaced labels, one row is enough"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "n = 5 (evenly spaced)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r n-20, fig.cap = "n = 20: 20 labels, split over two rows when one row is not enough"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 20)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "n = 20 (rows added automatically)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

When both `which` and `n` are given, `which` selects first and `n` then truncates the **result** to at most `n` labels, evenly spaced (`n` is a hard cap). With `which = NULL`, `n` picks evenly from all labels directly.

## Automatic behaviour: what happens when you pass nothing

**How the number of tracks (rows/columns) is chosen**: one row whenever the labels fit — they stretch along the axis, which gives short leader lines and the closest match to the `anno_mark()` look. More tracks are only added when the total width of the labels exceeds one row. If the labels crowd into a small stretch of the axis, the guide splits them over several rows even when their total width is small, using the span of that cluster, so that long crossing diagonals are avoided. At most `max_nrow` tracks (default `8`) are used.

With `which = NULL` and `n = NULL` the guide displays **all** labels by default. If the total width exceeds what `max_nrow` tracks can hold, the guide thins the labels out evenly and prints a **single** `cli` message, for example:

```{r auto-thin, fig.cap = "200 categories with neither which nor n: thinning keeps the plot readable, but fewer labels are shown"}
set.seed(1)
df200 <- data.frame(
  feature = factor(paste0("Feature", 1:200), levels = paste0("Feature", 1:200)),
  value = runif(200)
)

ggplot(df200, aes(x = feature, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.9) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "importance", title = "200 categories: automatic thinning") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

To silence that message (for example when plotting in a loop), set `options(ggutils.quiet = TRUE)`. Still, **always prefer an explicit `n =` or `which =`** so that you decide which labels are shown, rather than the screen size.

# Staggering over rows: `nrow`, `gap`, `padding`

`nrow` controls how many rows the x axis labels occupy below the axis; `NULL` (the default) means automatic — **one row whenever it fits**, more rows only when the labels crowd or overflow. `gap` is the space between rows (default `0.30`) and `padding` the minimum space between neighbouring label boxes in one row (default `0.25`); both are **relative to the label height**.

```{r nrow-1, fig.cap = "nrow = 1: everything in one row, the labels must fit"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 8, nrow = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "n = 8, nrow = 1") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r nrow-3, fig.cap = "nrow = 3: three staggered rows; more vertical space means more labels"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 24, nrow = 3)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "n = 24, nrow = 3") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r nrow-auto, fig.cap = "nrow = NULL: one row when it fits, otherwise rows are added automatically"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 30)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "n = 30, nrow = NULL (automatic rows)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

Rules of thumb:

- **Want more labels**: increase `nrow` (columns on a y axis, see below);
- **Rows look cramped**: increase `gap` and `padding` (e.g. `gap = 0.4`);
- **Labels clipped at the canvas edge**: `extend = 0` (the default) keeps every label box inside the panel, so this should not happen; only if you increase `extend` (to buy more layout freedom) do you also need a matching `theme(plot.margin = ...)`.

```{r tuned, fig.cap = "gap = 0.5, padding = 0.6: more space between rows and boxes"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 16, nrow = 2, gap = 0.5, padding = 0.6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "gap = 0.5, padding = 0.6") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

# Leader lines: `connection_style` and `link_length`

Whenever a label is **moved** (its position differs from its tick) the guide draws a leader line by default (`connection = TRUE`). There are three styles:

- `"diagonal"` (default): a short segment perpendicular to the axis, then a diagonal to the label's row, then another short perpendicular segment. This is the classic geometry of `circlize` and `ComplexHeatmap::anno_mark()` and stays readable with several rows;
- `"straight"`: one straight diagonal from the tick to the label box;
- `"elbow"`: a perpendicular segment followed by a shelf parallel to the axis.

```{r conn-diagonal, fig.cap = "connection_style = 'diagonal' (default): short stub + diagonal + short stub"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "connection_style = \"diagonal\" (default)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r conn-straight, fig.cap = "connection_style = 'straight': a single diagonal"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 2, connection_style = "straight")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "connection_style = \"straight\"") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r conn-elbow, fig.cap = "connection_style = 'elbow': a perpendicular segment plus a shelf"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 2, connection_style = "elbow")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "connection_style = \"elbow\"") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

`link_length` (default `3`, in millimetres) controls the length of the leader segment between the axis and the first row (column) of labels: decrease it when there are many rows and the lines get dense, increase it for roomier leader lines.

Colour, width and linetype of the lines are controlled by `connection_col`, `connection_lwd` (default `0.5`) and `connection_lty`; with `connection_col = NULL` (the default) the ticks' colour is used. Set `connection = FALSE` to turn leader lines off.

## Ticks: `tick`

`tick` controls the short tick marks next to the axis line:

- `"all"` (default): draw every tick, keeping the information that there are more categories;
- `"shown"`: only draw ticks for the labels that are displayed, a cleaner look;
- `"none"`: no ticks at all.

```{r tick-shown, fig.cap = "tick = 'shown': ticks only for the displayed labels"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2, tick = "shown")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "tick = \"shown\"") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

# y axis (vertical discrete axis)

Map the discrete variable to the y axis. Note that **`nrow` means columns on a y axis**: the labels are spread over several columns outside the axis, and the outermost column holds the labels that are pushed furthest out.

```{r y-axis, fig.cap = "y axis: nrow = 2 spreads the labels over 2 columns"}
labs40 <- paste0("Sample", 1:40)
df40 <- data.frame(
  sample = factor(labs40, levels = rev(labs40)),
  value = round(runif(40, 10, 100), 1)
)

ggplot(df40, aes(x = value, y = sample)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#F6903D", width = 0.8) +
  guides(y = guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "response", y = NULL, title = "y axis: n = 10, nrow = 2 (2 columns)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r y-axis-3, fig.cap = "y axis: nrow = 3, three columns make room for more labels"}
ggplot(df40, aes(x = value, y = sample)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#F6903D", width = 0.8) +
  guides(y = guide_axis_smart(which = seq(1, 40, by = 4), nrow = 3)) +
  labs(x = "response", y = NULL, title = "y axis: which = seq(1, 40, by = 4), nrow = 3") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```


# Radial coordinates: `coord_radial()`

`coord_radial()` renames the position scales to `theta` and `r`, so the guide is
attached with `guides(theta = ...)`.  On this axis `ggutils` lays the labels
out the way `circlize::circos.labels()` does: the text runs along the radius and
points towards the centre of the circle (turned around on the left half), crowded
labels are spread along the arc with the `smartAlign` algorithm, and every label
is tied to its tick by a three-segment leader line (radial stub, diagonal,
radial stub).

```{r radial-x, fig.cap = "coord_radial(theta = 'x'): a circular bar chart, every 4th label"}
ggplot(df50, aes(sample, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x") +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = seq(1, 50, by = 4)))
```

```{r radial-crowded, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 5.6, fig.cap = "12 crowded labels: spread along the arc and connected with three-segment leader lines"}
ggplot(df50, aes(sample, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x") +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = 9:20))
```

```{r radial-y, fig.cap = "categories mapped to y with theta = 'y' work the same way"}
ggplot(df50, aes(value, sample)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_radial(theta = "y") +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(n = 10))
```

```{r radial-half, fig.width = 9.6, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "a half circle (start/end) is laid out the same way"}
ggplot(df50, aes(sample, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", start = -0.5 * pi, end = 0.5 * pi) +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = 9:20))
```

## Circular heatmaps: labels outside or inside

With the bundled data (300 genes x 8 samples) the `theta` axis is the gene axis:

```{r radial-heat-outside, fig.width = 7.0, fig.height = 5.8, fig.cap = "circular heatmap with the labels outside: the crowded gene cluster spreads along the outer arc"}
data(airway_heatmap)
ggplot(airway_sample_z, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", inner.radius = 0.2) +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = airway_heatmap$mark)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)")
```

With a large inner radius the labels can go inside the hole
(`theta_side = "inside"`), attached to the inner radius:

```{r radial-heat-inside, fig.width = 7.0, fig.height = 5.0, fig.cap = "circular heatmap with the labels inside: theta_side = 'inside', attached to the inner radius"}
ggplot(airway_sample_z, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", inner.radius = 0.62) +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(
    which = airway_heatmap$mark, theta_side = "inside"
  )) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)")
```


## Facets: one circle per panel

With `facet_wrap()` / `facet_grid()` every panel is its own circle and lays its
labels out independently:

```{r radial-facet-wrap, fig.cap = "facet_wrap + coord_radial: one circle per panel, every 2nd label"}
d_facet <- data.frame(
  panel = rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 20),
  cat   = factor(rep(paste0("g", 1:20), 4), levels = paste0("g", 1:20)),
  value = round(runif(80, 5, 100), 1)
)
ggplot(d_facet, aes(cat, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3b82f6") +
  coord_radial(theta = "x") +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = seq(1, 20, by = 2))) +
  facet_wrap(~panel)
```

```{r radial-facet-free, fig.cap = "facet_wrap + free_x: each panel labels its own first 6 categories"}
d_free <- data.frame(
  panel = c(rep("A", 20), rep("B", 30)),
  cat   = factor(c(paste0("a", 1:20), paste0("b", 1:30))),
  value = round(runif(50, 5, 100), 1)
)
ggplot(d_free, aes(cat, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#f97316") +
  coord_radial(theta = "x") +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = 1:6)) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x")
```

```{r radial-facet-crowded, fig.cap = "a crowded cluster in every panel: spread independently per panel"}
d_crowd <- data.frame(
  panel = rep(c("set1", "set2"), each = 40),
  gene  = factor(rep(paste0("gene", 1:40), 2)),
  value = round(runif(80, 5, 100), 1)
)
ggplot(d_crowd, aes(gene, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#8b5cf6") +
  coord_radial(theta = "x") +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = c(5:16, 25:30))) +
  facet_wrap(~panel)
```

For a faceted circular heatmap add `scales = "free_x"`: each panel then uses its
own gene scale, so the ring is complete and the labels only land on the genes
that panel actually contains:

```{r radial-facet-heat, fig.width = 8.0, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "faceted circular heatmap + free_x: complete rings, each panel labels its own 4 genes"}
ggplot(airway_sample_z, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", inner.radius = 0.3) +
  guides(theta = guide_axis_smart(which = unlist(airway_heatmap$mark_by_set))) +
  facet_wrap(~gene_set, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)")
```

> Without `scales = "free_x"` the panels share one `theta` scale: half of each
> ring stays empty and the 8 genes picked by `which` are labelled in both panels.

Radial labels inherit the theme's axis text style (`axis.text.x` /
`axis.text.y`: size, colour, family, ...) exactly like the stock axis labels.

# Local annotations and heatmap labels (anno_mark style)

The `"diagonal"` geometry matches `circlize` and `ComplexHeatmap::anno_mark()` exactly: short stub, diagonal, short stub, text. Together with the track strategy ("one row when it fits, clustered labels split into tracks") this is ideal for **labelling only a few categories of interest**.

## Labels that sit in one stretch of the axis: automatic tracks

If the labels selected by `which` only occupy a small stretch of the axis, the guide splits them over several rows with vertical staggering, and every label still connects to its own tick:

```{r anno-cluster, fig.cap = "only labels 24-35 of 60 categories: split over several rows automatically"}
set.seed(5)
labs60 <- paste0("Sample", 1:60)
df60 <- data.frame(
  sample = factor(labs60, levels = labs60),
  value = round(runif(60, 10, 100), 1)
)

ggplot(df60, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = 24:35)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "which = 24:35 (several rows)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

To force the single-row, pure `anno_mark` look (labels stretched along the axis, longer leader lines), write `nrow = 1`:

```{r anno-cluster-nrow1, fig.cap = "the same labels with nrow = 1: stretched along the axis, longer leader lines"}
ggplot(df60, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = 24:35, nrow = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "which = 24:35, nrow = 1 (anno_mark style)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

## Heatmap labels: `sec.axis` + `dup_axis()`

"Label only a few rows and hide the rest" is the typical `anno_mark()` use case. Switch the main axis off, duplicate it with `dup_axis()`, and attach the smart guide to the copy.

This section uses the data set bundled with the package, **`airway_heatmap`**:
real RNA-seq from GEO
([GSE52778](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE52778);
human airway smooth muscle cells, four cell lines with and without
dexamethasone). The data is already processed — expressed genes only,
`log2(CPM + 1)`, the 300 most variable genes; heatmap examples below use
per-sample z-scores (each sample standardised across the genes), ordered by
hierarchical clustering (see `?airway_heatmap` for the exact steps) — so the
chunks below load it and plot immediately.

To make the leader lines and the vertical distribution of the labels visible,
the heatmap shows **300 genes** and labels 20 of them (12 neighbouring genes
from the top response cluster plus 8 scattered genes):

```{r anno-heatmap-data}
## bundled data: 300 genes x 8 samples, per-sample z-scores for the heat maps
data(airway_heatmap, package = "ggutils")
df_gene <- airway_sample_z
mark    <- airway_heatmap$mark
```

```{r anno-heatmap, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 10, fig.cap = "real data (GEO GSE52778), a tall 300-gene heatmap: only 20 genes are labelled, showing how the leader lines and the vertical label spacing are allocated"}
ggplot(df_gene, aes(x = sample, y = gene, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_y_discrete(
    guide = guide_none(),
    sec.axis = dup_axis(
      guide = guide_axis_smart(which = mark)
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "airway RNA-seq (GEO GSE52778), 300 genes") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

When the heatmap is faceted, every panel holds different data and lays out its
own labels. Here the genes are split into an "up" and a "down" panel, and each
panel labels only its four strongest responders (panel heights follow the number
of genes):

```{r anno-heatmap-facet, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 10, fig.cap = "faceted heatmap: each panel has different data and lays out its own labels"}
## the four strongest responders of each gene set are precomputed in the data
mark_facet <- unlist(airway_heatmap$mark_by_set, use.names = FALSE)

ggplot(df_gene, aes(x = sample, y = gene, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_grid(gene_set ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_y_discrete(
    position = "right",
    guide = guide_axis_smart(
      which = function(labels, positions) labels %in% mark_facet
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "facet by gene set, 300 genes") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Key points:

- single panel: hide all labels on the main axis with `guide = guide_none()` and
  put `guide_axis_smart()` on the axis created by `dup_axis()`;
- with hundreds of rows the effect is easiest to see: labels that crowd into the
  same strip are staggered vertically and each leader line goes back to its own
  row, while isolated labels get a longer horizontal line;
- **facets**: each panel selects and lays out its own labels independently; use a
  function for `which` (`function(labels, positions)`) so that every panel only
  matches the labels that exist in it;
- `dup_axis()` is not drawn per panel in a faceted plot; attach the smart guide
  directly with `scale_y_discrete(position = "right", guide = ...)` instead;
- `airway_heatmap` ships with the package (`data/airway_heatmap.rda`), so no
  `airway` or `SummarizedExperiment` dependency is needed at render time; the
  processing steps are documented in `?airway_heatmap` if you want to rebuild it
  from the original counts.

# Long labels and angles: `angle`, `hjust`, `vjust`

When the label text is long (for example "Sample12 (Treated A)"), staggering over rows may still not be enough; rotate the labels instead. `angle` accepts `0`, `45` and `90`; `NULL` (the default) inherits the angle from `axis.text.x` in the theme.

```{r long-rows, fig.cap = "long labels with staggered rows (no rotation): n = 12, nrow = 2"}
trt <- rep(c("Control", "Treated A", "Treated B"), 8)
labs24 <- paste0("Sample", 1:24, " (", trt, ")")
df24 <- data.frame(
  sample = factor(labs24, levels = labs24),
  value = round(runif(24, 10, 100), 1)
)

ggplot(df24, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Long labels, staggered rows: n = 12, nrow = 2") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r angle-45, fig.cap = "angle = 45 with nrow = 1, hjust = 1 and vjust = 1"}
ggplot(df24, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 1, angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

```{r angle-90, fig.cap = "angle = 90 with hjust = 1 and vjust = 0.5"}
ggplot(df24, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 1, angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

`hjust` / `vjust` are passed to the label text grob; with `NULL` the guide picks a sensible value for the angle. In practice:

- `angle = 0`: leave the defaults;
- `angle = 45`: `hjust = 1, vjust = 1` (right-aligned, next to the tick);
- `angle = 90`: `hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5`.

# Continuous axes work too

`guide_axis_smart()` does not require a discrete axis. With `scale_*_continuous(breaks = ...)` you can request many ticks and then show only a subset, over one or several rows:

```{r continuous, fig.cap = "continuous axis: 51 tick labels, only 10 displayed"}
set.seed(2024)
df_curve <- data.frame(
  x = seq(0, 100, length.out = 200),
  y = sin(seq(0, 100, length.out = 200) / 12) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.15)
)

ggplot(df_curve, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#5B8FF9", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 2), minor_breaks = NULL) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 10)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Continuous axis: 51 ticks, only 10 labels") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

On a continuous axis the character form of `which` matches the **formatted** tick text (e.g. `"20"`); for position-based rules the function form is more robust.

# Working with facets, coord_flip and themes

## facet: each panel lays out its own labels

Facetting gives every panel its own axis; the guide does its layout independently in each panel (a narrower panel may need more rows), and each panel only picks labels from its own breaks.

```{r facet, fig.cap = "facet_wrap: each panel lays out its labels independently"}
set.seed(7)
df_facet <- data.frame(
  sample = factor(paste0("Sample", 1:30), levels = paste0("Sample", 1:30)),
  value = round(runif(60, 10, 100), 1),
  group = rep(c("Group A", "Group B"), each = 30)
)

ggplot(df_facet, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, scales = "free_x") +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 6, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "facet_wrap: independent layout per panel") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

### Free scales: each panel labels only what it contains

With `scales = "free_x"` (or `free_y`) every panel carries different categories. Write all the labels you
want to mark once in `which`; each panel only draws the ones it actually has, and labels that are
**not present in a panel are skipped silently** (no error, no warning per panel):

```{r facet-free, fig.cap = "facet_wrap + free_x: each panel labels only its own categories"}
set.seed(8)
df_facet_free <- data.frame(
  cat = factor(
    c(paste0("A", 1:15), paste0("B", 1:15), paste0("C", 1:15), paste0("D", 1:15)),
    levels = c(paste0("A", 1:15), paste0("B", 1:15), paste0("C", 1:15), paste0("D", 1:15))
  ),
  value = round(runif(60, 10, 100), 1),
  group = rep(c("Group A", "Group B", "Group C", "Group D"), each = 15)
)
mark_facet_free <- c("A3", "A4", "A5", "A6", "B10", "C1", "C8", "D12")

ggplot(df_facet_free, aes(cat, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, nrow = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = mark_facet_free)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response",
       title = "facet_wrap + free_x: each panel labels what it has") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 11)
```

### Crowded labels inside one panel

A run of neighbouring labels is spread over several rows *inside that panel*; the narrower the panel,
the more rows are used. Here `nrow = 3` is forced:

```{r facet-crowded, fig.cap = "12 crowded labels inside a panel: spread over 3 rows"}
df_facet_crowd <- data.frame(
  cat = factor(paste0("c", 1:20), levels = paste0("c", 1:20)),
  value = rep(c(15, 62, 23, 78, 34, 51, 44, 29), length.out = 40),
  group = rep(c("Group A", "Group B"), each = 20)
)

ggplot(df_facet_crowd, aes(cat, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, nrow = 1) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = 3:14, nrow = 3)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response",
       title = "crowded labels inside a panel: 3 rows") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 11)
```

### facet_grid: a shared axis is drawn once, free axes once per panel

With `facet_grid` and a shared x axis the guide is drawn once; with `scales = "free_x"` every column gets its own:

```{r facet-grid, fig.cap = "facet_grid + free_x: each column labels its own categories"}
df_facet_grid <- data.frame(
  cat = factor(c(paste0("g", 1:15), paste0("h", 1:15)),
               levels = c(paste0("g", 1:15), paste0("h", 1:15))),
  value = round(runif(30, 10, 100), 1),
  side = rep(c("left panel", "right panel"), each = 15)
)

ggplot(df_facet_grid, aes(cat, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(. ~ side, scales = "free_x") +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(which = c("g2", "g7", "g12", "h3", "h9", "h14"))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response",
       title = "facet_grid + free_x: each column labels its own") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 11)
```

### Faceted heatmap: the right-hand y axis is labelled per panel

For a faceted heatmap attach the guide with `scale_y_discrete(position = "right")`; with `free_y` each panel
labels only the genes it contains, and a crowded run of genes is spread over rows inside that panel:

```{r facet-heatmap, fig.cap = "faceted heatmap: the bundled real data, each panel labels its own genes"}
## the real RNA-seq data bundled with the package (GEO GSE52778, 300 genes x 8 samples)
data(airway_heatmap, package = "ggutils")
df_facet_heat <- airway_sample_z
mark_wrap <- airway_heatmap$genes$gene[10:21]   # 12 neighbouring genes of the top cluster

ggplot(df_facet_heat, aes(sample, gene, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ gene_set, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_discrete(
    position = "right",
    guide = guide_axis_smart(which = mark_wrap)
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "faceted heatmap: each panel labels its own genes") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Facet checklist

- both `facet_wrap` and `facet_grid` work; the guide lays out inside every panel;
- `free_x` / `free_y`: each panel draws only the labels it has, so a single `which` can cover all panels;
- shared scales: the axis is drawn once (`facet_grid` rows share x, columns share y);
- crowding: a narrower panel uses more rows automatically, or force it with `nrow`;
- facets + `dup_axis()` do not work (the copy is not drawn per panel); attach the guide with
  `scale_*_discrete(position =, guide =)` instead.

## coord_flip: supported, but mapping to the y axis is recommended

`coord_flip()` has been superseded since ggplot2 4.0; map the discrete variable to the y axis instead (see above).

If old code still uses `coord_flip()`, **attach the guide to the scale**: in the flipped coordinate system `guides(x = ...)` looks up the guide by position, so it ends up on the numeric axis at the bottom instead of the discrete axis on the left. This spelling works:

```{r coord-flip, fig.cap = "after coord_flip(): the x labels become a vertical axis, the guide is attached to the scale"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis_smart(n = 10, nrow = 2)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "coord_flip: guide attached to the scale") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 12)
```

The equivalent spelling is `guides(y = guide_axis_smart(...))` — after flipping, the discrete axis's guide slot moves to `y`.

## theme: text styles are inherited

Colour, size, font family and face of the labels are inherited from `axis.text.x` / `axis.text.y`, so `theme()` code keeps working:

```{r theme, fig.cap = "label style inherited from axis.text.x: grey, 9 pt"}
ggplot(df50, aes(x = sample, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5B8FF9", width = 0.8) +
  guides(x = guide_axis_smart(n = 12, nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "response", title = "Label style inherited from the theme") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "grey30", size = 9))
```

Do **not** use `theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())` — the guide inherits that blank element verbatim and all labels disappear.

# `facet_gridn()`: a per-panel `facet_grid`

`facet_grid(scales = "free_x")` frees x **per column**: panels stacked in the same
column still share one x axis, because the layout sets `SCALE_X` to the column
index.  `facet_gridn()` lays the panels out exactly the same way (rows and
columns, row strips on the right, column strips on top) but sets `SCALE_X` /
`SCALE_Y` to the **panel** index, so every cell trains its own scale, gets its own
range and its own axis.

| `scales` | freedom | x axis | y axis |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"fixed"` | shared (default) | one global axis | one global axis |
| `"free_x"` | **per panel** | one axis per panel | one global axis |
| `"free_y"` | **per panel** | one global axis | one axis per panel |
| `"free"` | **per panel** | one axis per panel | one axis per panel |
| `"free_x_bycol"` | same as `facet_grid()` | one axis per column | one global axis |
| `"free_y_byrow"` | same as `facet_grid()` | one global axis | one axis per row |

The last two are compatibility values: `free_x_bycol` / `free_y_byrow` are exactly
the stock `free_x` / `free_y`, which is what you want when one figure has to mix
both kinds of freedom (x shared per column, y independent per panel).
`scales = "fixed"` matches `facet_grid()` pixel for pixel and can be swapped in
at any time.

All examples below use `mpg` (`drv`: 3 rows x `year`: 2 columns = 6 panels):

```{r gridn-setup-en}
library(patchwork)
d_cont <- mpg
d_disc <- mpg
d_disc$cylgrp <- factor(ifelse(d_disc$cyl == 4, "4 cyl", "6 / 8 cyl"),
                        levels = c("4 cyl", "6 / 8 cyl"))
th_n <- theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 9))
p_cont_n <- function(scales, fn = facet_gridn) {
  ggplot(d_cont, aes(displ, hwy)) +
    geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
    fn(vars(drv), vars(year), scales = scales) +
    labs(title = scales, x = NULL, y = NULL) + th_n
}
```

## Continuous axes: the four modes side by side

```{r gridn-cont-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=6.2, fig.cap="continuous axes, four scales: fixed shares everything, free_x / free_y free one direction per panel, free frees both"}
(p_cont_n("fixed")  | p_cont_n("free_x")) /
  (p_cont_n("free_y") | p_cont_n("free"))
```

With `free_x` every panel carries its own tick labels underneath, with `free_y`
every panel has its own ticks on the left, and `free` has both.  The difference is
measurable: on the same data the stock `facet_grid(scales = "free_x")` produces
only **2** distinct x ranges (one per column), `facet_gridn()` produces **6**
(one per panel); `free_y` is the mirror image -- 3 for stock (one per row), 6 for
`facet_gridn()`.

## Categorical x: every panel keeps only its own categories

In `mpg`, `2seater` only occurs in the `r` row and `minivan` only in the `f` row,
which makes "each panel keeps only its own categories" easy to see:

```{r gridn-catx-en}
p_catx_n <- function(fn = facet_gridn) {
  ggplot(d_cont, aes(class, hwy)) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "grey92", linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.8) +
    fn(vars(drv), vars(year), scales = "free_x") +
    th_n + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}
```

```{r gridn-catx-fig-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="facet_gridn(scales = 'free_x'): each panel's x axis lists only the categories it contains"}
p_catx_n()
```

```{r gridn-catx-stock-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="the same data with facet_grid(scales = 'free_x'): the x axis only sits under the bottom row, and a column shares its union"}
p_catx_n(facet_grid)
```

Compare the two: with `facet_gridn()` each panel's x categories are exactly the
ones that occur in that cell, while stock uses the union of the whole column, so
the 1999 cell of the `f` column still reserves a slot for `minivan` even though it
has no data there.

## Categorical y: the same rule, other direction

```{r gridn-caty-en}
p_caty_n <- function(fn = facet_gridn) {
  ggplot(d_cont, aes(hwy, class)) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "grey92", linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.8) +
    fn(vars(year), vars(drv), scales = "free_y") +
    th_n
}
```

```{r gridn-caty-fig-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="facet_gridn(scales = 'free_y'): each panel lists only its own categories on the left, with its own y axis"}
p_caty_n()
```

```{r gridn-caty-stock-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="facet_grid(scales = 'free_y'): the y axis only sits in the left-most column, and a row shares its union"}
p_caty_n(facet_grid)
```

## Discrete on both axes: everything per panel

```{r gridn-disc-en}
p_disc_n <- function(fn = facet_gridn) {
  ggplot(d_disc, aes(class, drv)) +
    geom_count(colour = "grey25", alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 6) +
    fn(vars(year), vars(cylgrp), scales = "free") +
    th_n + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}
```

```{r gridn-disc-fig-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="facet_gridn(scales = 'free'): both axes of every cell list only the categories it contains"}
p_disc_n()
```

```{r gridn-disc-stock-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="facet_grid(scales = 'free'): x per column, y per row, leaving unused categories on the axes"}
p_disc_n(facet_grid)
```

Counted per panel, the axis labels are x **6 / 7 / 5 / 7** and y **2 / 3 / 2 / 3**
for `facet_gridn()`, versus x **6 / 7 / 6 / 7** and y **3 / 3 / 3 / 3** for stock:
the 2008 cells have no `minivan` and the 4-cylinder cells have no rear-wheel drive,
and only `facet_gridn()` drops them from the axis.

## Panels in rows: `rows = vars(drv)`

Put the facet variable on `rows` and the layout becomes three rows of one column;
`free_y` gets easier to see, since each row draws only its own y range:

```{r gridn-rows-en, fig.width=6.6, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="rows = vars(drv), scales = 'free_y': every panel gets its own y axis"}
ggplot(d_cont, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_gridn(rows = vars(drv), cols = vars(year), scales = "free_y",
              space = "free_y") +
  th_n
```

`space = "free_y"` hands each row a height proportional to its y range; switch
back to `scales = "fixed"` for a shared axis.

## `space = "free_x"`: panel width follows its own range

```{r gridn-space-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="space = 'free_x': a wider x range gets a wider panel"}
ggplot(d_cont, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_gridn(vars(drv), vars(year), scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  th_n
```

`r/2008` is clearly wider than `f/1999`.  **Careful**: per-panel axes make the tick
labels differ in width from row to row, so column borders can drift slightly out
of alignment; keep the default `space = "fixed"` for a strictly tabular layout.

## Compatibility values: `free_x_bycol` / `free_y_byrow`

To keep the stock "per column / per row" semantics (say x shared per column but y
independent per panel), use these two values:

```{r gridn-bycol-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="free_x_bycol: the x axis only sits under the bottom row and is shared per column -- identical to facet_grid(scales = 'free_x')"}
p_cont_n("free_x_bycol")
```

`free_y_byrow` is the mirror image (y only in the left-most column, shared per row)
and matches the stock `free_y`.

```{r gridn-byrow-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="free_y_byrow: the y axis only sits on the left-most column and is shared per row -- identical to facet_grid(scales = 'free_y')"}
p_cont_n("free_y_byrow")
```


## Combining with the cluster tree

`scale_x_cluster()` / `scale_y_cluster()` read the facet's `scales` themselves, so
switching to `facet_gridn()` makes the trees per panel as well: one tree per cell,
without touching any tree-related code.  See "Cluster dendrogram on a discrete
axis" below for the examples.

# Spiral coordinates: `coord_spiral()`

`coord_spiral()` bends an ordinary Cartesian ggplot into an Archimedean
spiral. The geometry follows the **spiralize** package: the base spiral is
r = b·theta and one turn increases the radius by one unit. The x
aesthetic runs along the spiral as the angle, y becomes the radius inside the
track. Lines, bars, points and areas are supported, the matching angle and
radial axes are drawn automatically, and `facet_wrap()` / `facet_grid()` get
one spiral per panel.

```{r spiral-intro, fig.width = 5.8, fig.height = 5.6, fig.cap = "coord_spiral(): a line on three turns, with the angle and radial axes"}
set.seed(42)
d_sp <- data.frame(
  x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 300),
  y = sin(seq(0, 1, length.out = 300) * 8 * pi) * 0.35 + 0.5
)
ggplot(d_sp, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166ac", linewidth = 0.6) +
  coord_spiral() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "coord_spiral(): three turns")
```

The main arguments: `start` / `end` are degrees (`360 * n + a` means `n` turns
ending at `a`); `period` sets how many x units one turn covers; `height` is
the track height as a fraction of the gap between turns; `scale_by = "angle"`
(default) maps equal x steps to equal angles, while `"curve"` maps them to
equal lengths along the spiral. `clockwise`, `reverse` and `flip` control
direction, `labels = FALSE` turns the axes off, and `y_axis_theta` chooses
where the radial ruler is placed (the outer end by default).

```{r spiral-facet, fig.width = 10.67, fig.height = 4.1, fig.cap = "facet_wrap(): one spiral per panel, each with its own axis"}
d_sp$set <- rep(c("A", "B"), length.out = 300)
ggplot(d_sp, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~set) +
  coord_spiral(end = 360 + 90) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Two panels, two spirals") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
```

## Spiral heat map: 300 genes x 8 samples

A heat map is the most typical use of the spiral: genes run along the spiral (x) and
samples stack along the radius (y), with every `geom_tile()` cell bending with the
track.  This uses the package's built-in data, the same matrix as the circular heat
map above (GEO GSE52778, per-sample z-scores):

```{r spiral-heatmap, fig.width = 7.0, fig.height = 5.6, fig.cap = "The built-in data as a spiral heat map: 300 genes over four turns, with the eight samples as concentric bands"}
data(airway_heatmap)
d_hm <- airway_sample_z
d_hm$x <- as.numeric(d_hm$gene)
d_hm$y <- as.numeric(d_hm$sample)

ggplot(d_hm, aes(x, y, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "#f7f7f7", high = "#b2182b",
                       limits = c(-2.5, 2.5), oob = scales::squish, name = "z (sample)") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 4, height = .9, inner = .12, labels = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Three things matter:

- add **`expand = c(0, 0)`** on both scales, otherwise the colour band stops short of
  the track edges and leaves white slivers at the start and the end;
- make **`inner` larger**; the default `0.04` leaves the innermost turn so small that
  the cells pile up, `0.10 - 0.12` works well;
- for four turns or more use **`labels = FALSE`** - 300 gene ticks mean nothing; turn
  them back on at two turns, where the radial ticks label the samples.
To label the samples on the radius instead, use two turns, keep the axis and
replace the y breaks with the sample names:

```r
ggplot(d_hm, aes(x, y, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), breaks = 1:8,
                     labels = paste0("S", 1:8)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 2, height = .85, inner = .1)
```

## An arrow along the spiral (`spiral_arrow()` style)

`spiralize`'s `spiral_arrow(0.2, 0.8)` is just **an x interval interpolated into a
`geom_path()` along the track**, plus an arrow head.  `geom_path()` is essential: it
connects the interpolated points in data order, so the line follows the spiral;
`geom_segment()` only has two end points and would cut straight across the panel.

```{r spiral-arrow, fig.width = 5.2, fig.height = 4.7, fig.cap = "An arrow along the spiral from x = 0.2 to 0.8, with minor ticks between the labelled ones"}
d_arrow <- data.frame(x = seq(0.2, 0.8, length.out = 900), y = 0.5)

ggplot(d_arrow, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 2.6, colour = "#e41a1c", lineend = "round",
            arrow = grid::arrow(length = unit(5.5, "mm"), type = "closed")) +
  scale_x_spiral_axis(breaks = seq(0.2, 0.8, by = 0.05),
                      minor_breaks = seq(0.2, 0.8, by = 0.0125),
                      label_size = 5) +
  scale_y_spiral_axis(show = FALSE) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 3, height = .78, inner = .06, outer = .46, y_axis = FALSE)
```

The numbers are not arbitrary: `linewidth = 2.6` mm is about 60% of the track, so the
red band sits inside it; `minor_breaks` every 0.0125 puts four small ticks between two
labelled ones, the way `spiralize` draws major ticks with labels and minor ticks
without.  For the opposite direction use `scale_x_reverse()`.


# Which layers are supported

`coord_spiral()` is an ordinary ggproto `Coord`: all it does is map every point
from the data scale to panel coordinates.  So **any layer that hands its `x`/`y`
to the coordinate transform just works**, with no extra setup.

| Layer | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `geom_point()` / `geom_jitter()` | works | points land on the track |
| `geom_line()` / `geom_step()` | works | the line is bent along the spiral |
| `geom_path()` | works | connects in data order, so an unordered path loops back |
| `geom_area()` / `geom_ribbon()` | works | both bounds follow the spiral |
| `geom_col()` / `geom_bar()` | works | bars become wedges of the track |
| `geom_histogram()` / `geom_density()` | works | binning and density are fine |
| `geom_smooth()` | works | curve and confidence band both follow the spiral |
| `geom_tile()` | works | heat maps unroll along the spiral (below) |
| `geom_boxplot()` / `geom_violin()` | works | needs a discrete x |
| `geom_text()` / `geom_label()` | works | keep the font small, or the text spans turns |
| `geom_errorbar()` / `geom_pointrange()` / `geom_linerange()` | works | whiskers become short arcs on the track |
| `geom_polygon()` | works | vertices are mapped, edges are straight (see below) |
| `geom_raster()` | falls back | warns that it needs a linear coord and draws via `geom_rect()` |
| `geom_segment()` / `geom_curve()` | works | both ends are transformed, arrows (`arrow =`) included; the edge between them is straight, invisible over short spans |
| `geom_rect()` | works | all four corners are transformed, giving a quad that hugs the track |
| `geom_hline()` / `geom_vline()` / `geom_abline()` | not supported | an infinite line has no end points to transform, so it turns into a closed shape |
| `geom_sf()` / `geom_map()` | not supported | they need `coord_sf()` / their own coord |

```{r spiral-geoms, fig.cap = "ggplot2's own layer examples drawn on coord_spiral(): points, line, area, bars, histogram, smooth, boxplot, heat map, text", fig.width = 8.4, fig.height = 7.4}
library(patchwork)

## the layer examples are the ones from the ggplot2 reference pages
sp <- function(p, title) {
  p + coord_spiral(turns = 3, labels = FALSE) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = title) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9),
          axis.text = element_text(size = 5),
          legend.position = "none")
}

wrap_plots(
  sp(ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) + geom_point(), "geom_point()"),
  sp(ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) + geom_line(), "geom_line()"),
  sp(ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) + geom_area(fill = "#9ecae1"), "geom_area()"),
  sp(ggplot(mpg, aes(class, hwy)) + geom_col(), "geom_col()"),
  sp(ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2), "geom_histogram()"),
  sp(ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(), "geom_smooth()"),
  sp(ggplot(mpg, aes(class, hwy)) + geom_boxplot(), "geom_boxplot()"),
  sp(ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
       geom_tile(), "geom_tile()"),
  sp(ggplot(mpg[seq(1, 234, 12), ], aes(displ, hwy, label = cyl)) +
       geom_text(size = 2), "geom_text()"),
  ncol = 3
)
```


**Why the edges between two points are straight**: the transform is applied to every
position aesthetic (`x`, `y`, `xend`, `yend`, `xmin`, `xmax`, `ymin`, `ymax`), but the
edge between two transformed points is still a straight segment.  Over a short span
you cannot see the difference - the figure below is a copy of
`spiralize::spiral_segments()`, where every segment spans only 0.02 x units and looks
like it lies exactly on the track.  Over a long span the chord becomes visible; in
that case draw the line with `geom_path()` instead, interpolating intermediate points
along the arc and separating the pieces with `group`.

```{r spiral-segments, fig.width = 8.4, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "A copy of spiralize's Segments example: coloured segments on the left, segments with arrow heads on the right"}
set.seed(2)
n <- 400
d_seg <- data.frame(
  x  = runif(n), y = runif(n)
)
d_seg$xend <- d_seg$x + runif(n, min = -0.01, max = 0.01)
d_seg$yend <- 1 - d_seg$y
d_seg$col <- grDevices::hcl.colors(n, "Dark 3")

p_seg <- ggplot(d_seg, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = d_seg$col,
               linewidth = .6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 4, height = .85, labels = FALSE)

p_arrow <- ggplot(d_seg[seq_len(120), ], aes(x, y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = d_seg$col[seq_len(120)],
               linewidth = .6, show.legend = FALSE,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"))) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 4, height = .85, labels = FALSE)

wrap_plots(p_seg, p_arrow, ncol = 2)
```

## Radial and stacked bars

The `spiralize::spiral_bars()` look comes straight out of `geom_col()`: bars grow
from the smallest y (usually 0) towards the outside, and `width` sets how much of
the angle they take.  Setting `expand` to 0 makes the bars fill the track, with no
gap before the first one or after the last one.

```{r spiral-bars, fig.width = 7.4, fig.height = 4.0, fig.cap = "Left: one bar per column. Right: the same data stacked"}
set.seed(1)

## one value per column
d1 <- data.frame(x = seq_len(240), v = runif(240, .05, 1))
p1 <- ggplot(d1, aes(x, v)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, fill = "grey20") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 3, height = .8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "one column: geom_col()")

## a matrix: one column per stack
n <- 200
m <- matrix(runif(3 * n), ncol = 3)
m <- m / rowSums(m)
d2 <- data.frame(x = rep(seq_len(n), 3),
                 stack = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = n)),
                 v = as.vector(m))
p2 <- ggplot(d2, aes(x, v, fill = stack)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#4C72B0", "#DD8452", "#55A868")) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_spiral(turns = 3, height = .8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "matrix columns: stacked")

wrap_plots(p1, p2, ncol = 2) &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10), legend.position = "bottom")
```

Stacking works because y *is* the radius inside the track: `position = "stack"`
stacks the pieces along the radius, so every column of the matrix becomes one
concentric band.  In the same way `position = "dodge"` spreads the bars along the
angle, and `position = "fill"` normalises them to the track width.

# Cluster dendrogram on a discrete axis

`guide_axis_cluster()` adds a hierarchical clustering dendrogram to an x or y
discrete axis; the companion `scale_x_cluster()` / `scale_y_cluster()` reorder the
categories into dendrogram leaf order. The key point: the companion scale sets
`limits` to the clustered order, so **both the axis labels and the data in the
plot are reordered together** and the tree stays aligned with the data -- there
is no "labels changed but cells stayed put" mismatch.

```{r cluster-tree-setup-en}
set.seed(1)
mat <- matrix(rnorm(12 * 4), nrow = 12,
              dimnames = list(paste0("g", 1:12), paste0("s", 1:4)))
long <- as.data.frame(as.table(mat))
names(long) <- c("gene", "sample", "value")
```

A rectangular dendrogram on the y axis (`type = "rectangle"`, the default);
`method` selects the clustering method, `height` is the overall tree height in
centimetres, and `col` sets the line colour:

```{r cluster-tree-y-en, fig.width=6, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Rectangular cluster tree on the y axis; genes are reordered by clustering"}
ggplot(long, aes(sample, gene, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_y_cluster(mat, method = "average", height = 1.4, col = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The triangular tree (`type = "triangle"`) converges to a single vertex at every
merge, drawn like `plot(as.dendrogram(hc), type = "triangle")`:

```{r cluster-tree-triangle-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Triangular cluster tree on the x axis"}
ggplot(long, aes(gene, sample, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_x_cluster(mat, method = "ward.D2", height = 1.4,
                  col = "#b2182b", type = "triangle") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## `method`: a different linkage, a different tree

`method` goes straight to `stats::hclust()`.  The two figures above use `average`
and `ward.D2`; switch to `"single"` (nearest-neighbour chaining) and the tree
collapses into a chain, with the leaves re-ordered as well:

```{r cluster-method-single-en, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="method = 'single': chaining gives a visibly different tree from average / ward.D2"}
ggplot(long, aes(sample, gene, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_y_cluster(mat, method = "single", height = 1.4, col = "#7b3294") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## A tree on both axes

`scale_x_cluster()` clusters the columns, `scale_y_cluster()` the rows; the two
trees stay out of each other's way and both axes are re-ordered:

```{r cluster-both-axes-en, fig.width=6.6, fig.height=5.6, fig.cap="x tree on top, y tree on the left: rows and columns both in cluster order"}
ggplot(long, aes(gene, sample, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 1.1) +
  scale_y_cluster(position = "left", height = 1.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

To get just the clustered order without the companion scale, use
`cluster_order()`, e.g. `scale_y_discrete(limits = cluster_order(mat))`.

## `position`: move the tree, not the labels

`position` decides **which side the tree is drawn on**; the labels never move:

| axis | `position` | tree | labels |
|---|---|---|---|
| x | `"bottom"` (default) | outside the labels, by the `gene` title | still at the bottom |
| x | `"top"` | above the panel; with facets, **under the strip** | still at the bottom |
| y | `"left"` (default) | left of the labels | still on the left |
| y | `"right"` | at the end of the panel row | still on the left |

```{r cluster-pos-helpers-en}
tile_x <- function(pos) {
  ggplot(long, aes(gene, sample, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                         midpoint = 0) +
    scale_x_cluster(position = pos, height = 1) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
}
tile_y <- function(pos) {
  ggplot(long, aes(sample, gene, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                         midpoint = 0) +
    scale_y_cluster(position = pos, height = 1) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
}
```

x tree on top, labels still at the bottom:

```{r cluster-pos-top-en, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="position = 'top': tree above the panel, x labels stay at the bottom"}
tile_x("top")
```

y tree on the left, left of the labels:

```{r cluster-pos-left-en, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="position = 'left': tree left of the y labels"}
tile_y("left")
```

y tree on the right, at the end of the panel row:

```{r cluster-pos-right-en, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="position = 'right': tree to the right of the panel"}
tile_y("right")
```

The tree can leave the labels because it no longer goes through a secondary
axis: it is drawn straight into the final gtable, the only place that knows the
geometry of every panel. That is also why `facet_grid()` works -- row facets own
the y axis and column facets own the x axis, so each tree lands under its own
strip.

## No matrix needed

None of the examples above pass a matrix: `scale_x_cluster()` /
`scale_y_cluster()` derive it at draw time from the plot's own data -- the focal
axis becomes the rows, the other positional axis the columns, and the first
numeric aesthetic (`fill`, `colour`, `size`, ...) the value. To cluster on
another column, say `value =`:

```{r cluster-value-en, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(d, aes(gene, sample, fill = zscore, size = pct)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_cluster(value = "zscore")   # defaults to the first numeric aesthetic
```

Changing `value =` changes the tree as well.  The dot plot below carries both
`fill` (expression) and `size` (fraction expressed); clustering on one or the
other gives different trees:

```{r cluster-value-demo-en, fig.width=9.4, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="One dot plot, clustered on fill (left) and on size (right): the trees differ"}
set.seed(7)
d_val <- expand.grid(gene = paste0("g", 1:12), sample = paste0("s", 1:6))
d_val$zscore <- stats::rnorm(nrow(d_val))
d_val$pct <- stats::runif(nrow(d_val), 0, 1)
p_val <- function(v) {
  ggplot(d_val, aes(gene, sample, fill = zscore, size = pct)) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, colour = "grey25") +
    scale_x_cluster(value = v, height = 1.1) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b") +
    labs(title = paste0("value = \"", v, "\"")) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 10)
}
wrap_plots(p_val("zscore"), p_val("pct"), nrow = 1)
```

## Facets: one tree per panel

A single-cell dot plot is usually faceted by cell type, and every panel holds a
different gene set. Hand `scales` to the facet and the tree is recomputed per
panel automatically -- no `free = TRUE` needed:

```{r cluster-dot-setup-en}
data(pbmc3k_dotplot)
d4 <- droplevels(pbmc3k_dotplot[pbmc3k_dotplot$celltype %in%
                                  c("Naive CD4 T", "CD14+ Mono", "NK", "B"), ])
d4$cluster_id <- factor(d4$cluster_id)      # cluster id on y: 0 / 1 / 3 / 6
top_of <- function(x, k) head(x$gene[order(-x$avg_exp_scaled)], k)

dot_layers <- function() {
  list(
    geom_point(aes(size = pct_expressed, fill = avg_exp_scaled),
               shape = 21, colour = "black", stroke = 0.25),
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "#f7f7f7", high = "#b2182b"),
    theme_bw(base_size = 10),
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
  )
}

genes_by_ct <- lapply(split(d4, d4$celltype), top_of, k = 4)
d_panel <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(genes_by_ct), function(ct) {
  x <- d4[d4$gene %in% genes_by_ct[[ct]], ]
  x$panel <- ct
  x
}))
d_panel$panel <- factor(d_panel$panel, levels = names(genes_by_ct))
```

```{r cluster-dot-facet-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=8.4, fig.cap="facet_wrap(scales = 'free_x'): one x tree per panel, tucked under its own strip"}
ggplot(d_panel, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.9) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## The four `scales` modes: when the tree is recomputed

`facet_wrap()` / `facet_grid()` `scales` are picked up automatically; whether the
tree is recomputed per panel depends only on whether that axis is free:

| `scales` | x axis | y axis | x tree | y tree |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"fixed"` | shared | shared | one tree for all panels | one per axis |
| `"free_x"` | per panel | shared | one per panel column | one per axis |
| `"free_y"` | shared | per panel | one tree for all panels | one per panel row |
| `"free"` | per panel | per panel | one per panel column | one per panel row |

```{r cluster-dot-xy-en}
sets <- list("All four" = c("Naive CD4 T", "CD14+ Mono", "NK", "B"),
             "T + Mono" = c("Naive CD4 T", "CD14+ Mono"),
             "NK + B"   = c("NK", "B"))
d_xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets), function(p) {
  x <- d4[d4$celltype %in% sets[[p]] & d4$gene %in% genes_by_ct[[sets[[p]][1]]], ]
  x$panel <- p
  x
}))
d_xy$panel <- factor(d_xy$panel, levels = names(sets))
```

By default the tree is inserted **between the strip and the panel**, with a
small gap to the strip (`options(ggutils.tree_gap = 0.14)`, centimetres).  Add
`strip_side` to move it outside the strip instead:

```{r cluster-strip-side-en, eval = FALSE}
scale_x_cluster(position = "top", strip_side = "above")
```

```{r cluster-strip-above-en, fig.width=9.2, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="strip_side = 'above': the tree moves outside the strip, which stays flush with the panel"}
ggplot(d_xy, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.9, strip_side = "above") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

`free_x`: each panel has its own gene set, so each x tree is computed on its own,
while the y axis stays shared:

```{r cluster-scales-freex-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.6, fig.cap="scales = 'free_x': per-panel x trees"}
ggplot(d_xy, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.9)
```

`free_y`: x shared, y per panel, and the y tree becomes one per panel as well,
hugging its own cluster labels:

```{r cluster-scales-freey-en, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="scales = 'free_y': shared x tree, per-panel y trees"}
ggplot(d_xy, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.9) +
  scale_y_cluster(position = "left", height = 0.9)
```

Freeing both directions *and* adding a y tree squeezes the panels very thin;
usually keep one direction. See the acceptance report in the package for the
full comparison.

## Multi-row facets: each row owns its own strip

With `nrow = 2` the trees are inserted row by row, so the second row's trees never
bleed into the first:

```{r cluster-nrow2-en}
## four panels of two cell types each (= two clusters), same size, to show the layout
sets2 <- list("T + Mono"  = c("Naive CD4 T", "CD14+ Mono"),
              "NK + B"    = c("NK", "B"),
              "Mono + B"  = c("CD14+ Mono", "B"),
              "T + NK"    = c("Naive CD4 T", "NK"))
d_grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets2), function(p) {
  x <- d4[d4$celltype %in% sets2[[p]] & d4$gene %in% genes_by_ct[[sets2[[p]][1]]], ]
  x$panel <- p
  x
}))
d_grid$panel <- factor(d_grid$panel, levels = names(sets2))
```

```{r cluster-nrow2-fig-en, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7, fig.cap="facet_wrap(nrow = 2): the 4 x trees land under their own panel's strip"}
ggplot(d_grid, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free", nrow = 2) +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.8)
```

## `facet_grid()`: rows own y, columns own x

In `facet_grid()` the row facet decides y and the column facet decides x, so the
**x tree sits under the column strip and the y tree on the left of each row**.
Add two categorical columns and build a 2x2: `grp` splits the clusters in two
(rows) and `prog` splits the genes into two marker sets (columns):

```{r cluster-grid-data-en}
prog_a <- unique(unlist(lapply(c("Naive CD4 T", "CD14+ Mono"),
                               function(ct) top_of(d4[d4$celltype == ct, ], 3))))
prog_b <- unique(unlist(lapply(c("NK", "B"),
                               function(ct) top_of(d4[d4$celltype == ct, ], 3))))
d_fg <- d4[d4$gene %in% c(prog_a, prog_b), ]
d_fg$grp <- factor(ifelse(as.character(d_fg$cluster_id) %in% c("0", "1"),
                          "c0 / c1", "c3 / c6"), levels = c("c0 / c1", "c3 / c6"))
d_fg$prog <- factor(ifelse(d_fg$gene %in% prog_a, "T / Mono", "NK / B"),
                    levels = c("T / Mono", "NK / B"))
```

```{r cluster-grid-fig-en, fig.width=8.6, fig.height=7, fig.cap="facet_grid(grp ~ prog): x tree under the column strip, y tree left of each row"}
ggplot(d_fg, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_grid(grp ~ prog, scales = "fixed", drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.8) +
  scale_y_cluster(position = "left", height = 0.8)
```

Two things to keep in mind: `drop = FALSE` is there **to make `fixed` visible** --
a discrete y axis drops empty levels per panel by default, and once it does,
`fixed` and `free_y` look identical; without dropping, `fixed` tiles all clusters
into every panel. And **the number of y trees does not change with `free` inside
`facet_grid()`**, because the row itself is the y facet, so every row always has
one y axis -- `fixed` vs `free_y` only changes how many leaves a tree has.

## An RNA-seq heatmap: faceted by gene set, one y tree per panel

Real RNA-seq heatmaps are usually split by gene set (up / down), and each facet
holds entirely different genes -- the textbook case for per-panel trees.  The
bundled `airway_heatmap` (dexamethasone-treated human airway smooth muscle cells,
300 variable genes x 8 samples) is used below.  The data already carries a
The bundled matrix is a per-gene row z-score; below every sample is
**standardised again across the 300 genes** (`scale()` works column-wise), giving
`z_sample`, so `fill = z_sample` with `scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 0)` draws the
standard red/blue heatmap.

Below: the 18 strongest genes of each set, faceted by `gene_set` with
`scales = "free_y"` so every panel lays out only its own genes -- and therefore
gets its own y tree.  The sample axis gets one x tree, which clusters the
treatment and control samples into two branches:

```{r cluster-heat-facet-setup-en}
data(airway_heatmap, package = "ggutils")
gs <- airway_heatmap$genes
top_set <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(gs, gs$gene_set), function(d) {
  head(d[order(-abs(d$delta)), ], 18)
}))
d_hm <- droplevels(airway_sample_z[airway_sample_z$gene %in% top_set$gene, ])
```

```{r cluster-heat-facet-en, fig.width=8.6, fig.height=6.8, fig.cap="Airway heatmap faceted by gene set: one y tree per panel plus a sample x tree on top"}
ggplot(d_hm, aes(sample, gene, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ gene_set, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.8, col = "grey25") +
  scale_y_cluster(position = "left", height = 1.2, col = "grey25") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

With `fixed` the two panels share one gene axis and each wastes a large empty
block; `free_y` plus a per-panel tree is what this "different genes per facet"
data asks for.  The x axis is shared, so the sample tree is drawn once and lines
up with both panels.

## Radial coordinates: ring trees on the theta axis, arc tree on the r axis

Around a circle there is no "row above the panel" to put a tree in, so on a
`coord_radial()` theta axis `scale_x_cluster()` draws a **ring dendrogram**:
leaves sit on a ring, every merge is an arc at another radius joined to its
children by radial stubs (`type = "triangle"` uses straight chords to the merge
point instead).  The labels keep their normal `guide_axis_theta()` look.

`position` decides which side the ring tree goes to:

| `position` | tree drawn | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"bottom"` (default) | **inside the hole** | leaves on the inner circle, merges towards the centre; needs `inner.radius > 0`, a pie without a hole is skipped |
| `"top"` | **outside the circle** | leaves on the outer circle, merges outwards; `ring_gap` is measured from the labels and the panel is padded automatically |

Ring tree inside the hole (a donut heat map):

```{r cluster-ring-inner-en, fig.width=8, fig.height=7.4, fig.cap="coord_radial(inner.radius = 0.55) + position = 'bottom': tree inside the hole, merges towards the centre"}
data(airway_heatmap, package = "ggutils")
d_ring <- droplevels(
  airway_sample_z[airway_sample_z$gene %in% unique(airway_sample_z$gene)[1:30], ]
)
ggplot(d_ring, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", inner.radius = 0.55) +
  scale_x_cluster(method = "ward.D2", height = 1.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 8) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, "cm"),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

`position = "top"` puts the same tree outside the circle; the leaf ring starts
after the labels and the panel gets extra room automatically:

```{r cluster-ring-outer-en, fig.width=8, fig.height=7.8, fig.cap="coord_radial() + position = 'top': tree outside the circle, merges outwards"}
ggplot(d_ring, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x") +
  scale_x_cluster(method = "ward.D2", height = 1, position = "top") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
