```{r cluster-ring-outer-en, fig.width=8, fig.height=7.8, fig.cap="coord_radial() + position = 'top': tree outside the circle, merges outwards"}
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 8) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, "cm"),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Facets work like the cartesian ones -- one tree per panel, clustered from that
panel's own genes when the theta scale is free (`free_x` / `free`):

```{r cluster-ring-facet-en, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="facet_wrap(scales = 'free_x') + coord_radial: one inner ring tree per panel"}
d_ring2 <- droplevels(
  airway_sample_z[airway_sample_z$gene %in% unique(airway_sample_z$gene)[1:60], ]
)
ggplot(d_ring2, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ gene_set, scales = "free_x") +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", inner.radius = 0.45) +
  scale_x_cluster(method = "ward.D2", height = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 7) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 0.4, "cm"),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

### Arc tree on the r (y) axis

On a full circle the r axis is just a column of labels, so `scale_y_cluster()`
draws **no** tree there.  With a partial arc (`start` / `end`) ggplot2 puts the
sample labels on a radial ray, and `scale_y_cluster()` then draws an
**arc-shaped wedge tree** at the other end of the arc -- the side without
labels:

- leaf position -> radius: every sample lines up with its own ring;
- merge height -> angle: `height` sets the angular width
  (`min(pi/3, 0.30 * height)` radians);
- equal-height branches are concentric arcs and the leaf stubs hug the tiles,
  so the whole tree is made of arcs.

```{r cluster-ring-y-en, fig.width=8, fig.height=6.2, fig.cap="180 degree arc + scale_y_cluster(): arc tree at the label-free end of the arc"}
d_ring_y <- droplevels(
  airway_sample_z[airway_sample_z$gene %in% unique(airway_sample_z$gene)[1:16], ]
)
ggplot(d_ring_y, aes(gene, sample, fill = z_sample)) +
  geom_tile() +
  coord_radial(theta = "x", start = -0.5 * pi, end = 0.5 * pi,
               inner.radius = 0.55) +
  scale_y_cluster(method = "ward.D2", height = 1.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "z-score (sample)") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 8) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, "cm"),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

90/270 degree arcs work the same way, only `start` / `end` change, and the
r-axis tree can be combined with an x tree on the same plot.

## Facet scales: the trees follow the facet

The previous sections all used `facet_wrap()`.  Switching to `facet_grid()` or
`facet_gridn()` needs no `free = TRUE`: `scale_*_cluster()` reads the facet's
`scales` directly, and whether the tree is per panel depends only on whether that
axis is free (the six `scales` values of both facets are tabulated in
"`facet_gridn()`: a per-panel `facet_grid`" above).

`facet_gridn(scales = "free_x")` is per panel, so every cell gets its own x tree:

```{r cluster-gridn-fig-en, fig.width=9.2, fig.height=5.0, fig.cap="facet_gridn(scales = 'free_x'): every panel gets its own x axis and its own x tree"}
ggplot(d_xy, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_gridn(cols = vars(panel), scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.9) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

Switch to `scales = "free"` and add `scale_y_cluster()` to get one x tree and one
y tree **per cell**:

```{r cluster-gridn-both-en, fig.width=9.6, fig.height=6.0, fig.cap="facet_gridn(scales = 'free'): per-panel x and y trees"}
ggplot(d_xy, aes(gene, cluster_id)) + dot_layers() +
  facet_gridn(cols = vars(panel), scales = "free") +
  scale_x_cluster(position = "top", height = 0.9) +
  scale_y_cluster(position = "left", height = 0.9) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## Limits of the cluster tree

- **`position` only moves the tree.** To move the labels as well, use the usual
  `scale_x_discrete(position = "top")`; the two do not affect each other.
- **No tree when the facets map categories one to one.** A panel left with a
  single category (e.g. faceting by a cell type that is one-to-one with the
  cluster) has nothing to cluster and the tree is left blank.
- **Freeing both directions and drawing both trees flattens the panels**, because
  every y axis needs a column of its own. To see x and y at once, reduce `height`
  first, or keep a single direction.
- **An explicit matrix cannot be reordered per panel**: the tree falls back to a
  conservative "merge adjacent groups only" shape, which may look different from
  `hclust()`.
- **On a short canvas the panels collapse to zero height.** The tree row is a
  fixed height (`height` in cm), so with several panel rows on a small device
  (e.g. two rows in 4 inches) the fixed rows eat the `1null` panel rows and only
  the trees and axis text remain. Increase `fig.height` (leave 2-3 cm per panel
  row), use fewer panel rows, or lower `height`.

# Known limitations and tuning advice

- **It can only pick existing ticks, never add new ones.** If a category is not in the scale's breaks, `which` cannot select it — add it first with `scale_x_discrete(breaks = ...)`.
- **Automatic rows are on demand.** One row whenever it fits (stretched along the axis, closest to the `anno_mark()` look); more rows only when the width overflows or the labels cluster, capped at `max_nrow` tracks. Write `nrow = 1` explicitly for the pure single-row `anno_mark` look.
- **Fewer labels than requested is possible.** On a narrow panel, or with too few rows, the guide drops labels by priority — it never draws overlapping labels. To show more, add `nrow`, make the figure larger, or reduce `padding`/`gap`.
- **Automatic thinning when `which = NULL` and `n = NULL`.** When the total width exceeds what `max_nrow` tracks can hold, the guide thins evenly and prints one `cli` message; `options(ggutils.quiet = TRUE)` silences it. Always prefer explicit `n =` or `which =`.
- **The automatic number of rows depends on the device.** The same plot may use a different number of rows in the RStudio window and in a 1600x900 PNG. For reproducible output write `nrow` explicitly, or tell the guide the panel width with `panel_width` (in cm).
- **`angle` is best combined with `nrow = 1`.** Rotated labels need more vertical space (the guide reserves the rotated bounding box), and stacking rotated labels is rarely worth it.
- **Never blank the labels with `axis.text.*`**: the guide inherits the blank element and draws no text; to hide labels, do not use the guide at all.
- **`coord_flip()` is superseded**: for new code map the discrete variable to the y axis. In old code attach the guide to the scale (`scale_x_discrete(guide = ...)`) or use `guides(y = ...)`; `guides(x = ...)` lands on the numeric axis after flipping.
- **`plot.margin` is only needed when `extend > 0`**: with the default `extend = 0` labels never leave the panel and are never clipped; if you increase `extend`, reserve the matching margin with `theme(plot.margin = ...)`.
- **Custom secondary axes**: `sec.axis = dup_axis(guide = guide_axis_smart(...))` is verified (see the "Local annotations and heatmap labels" section); check more involved secondary axes on a small plot first.
- Performance is not a concern: label measurement happens once at build time, and 200 categories are interactive-fast.
